lessons.title: Modes of Transportation
lessons.body: In East Africa, getting around means knowing your matatu from your boda boda. A matatu is a minibus taxi, common in Kenya and Tanzania. In Uganda, they call them taxis. Fares depend on distance and time of day. For example, in Nairobi, a matatu from CBD to Westlands costs around 50-100 KSh. Boda bodas are motorcycle taxisâfast but risky. Always agree on the price before you hop on. In Tanzania, you'll find daladalas (minibuses) and bajajis (three-wheeled tuk-tuks). Bajajis are cheaper than taxis for short trips, often 2000-5000 TSh. For longer journeys, buses like Modern Coast or Tahmeed run between major cities. A bus from Nairobi to Mombasa takes about 8 hours and costs 1000-1500 KSh. Trains are limited but scenic: the TAZARA railway from Dar es Salaam to Zambia, or the new SGR from Nairobi to Mombasa. Boats are essential in places like Zanzibar or Lake Victoria. Always carry small billsâconductors rarely have change. Learn key phrases: 'Ningependa kwenda...' (I would like to go to...), 'Bei ni ngapi?' (How much is it?), 'Shusha hapa' (Stop here). Safety tip: avoid unlicensed taxis; use apps like Uber or Bolt in cities. In rural areas, pick-up trucks (malori) often carry passengers in the backâcheap but uncomfortable. Remember, 'safari' means journey, not just wildlife tour. So when someone says 'safari njema,' they wish you a good trip.

lessons.title: Buying Tickets and Making Reservations
lessons.body: Buying tickets in East Africa can be done at the station, online, or through a mobile app. For buses, companies like Easy Coach, Modern Coast, and Tahmeed have websites or agents. You can also use platforms like BuuPass or QuickBus in Kenya. A ticket from Nairobi to Kisumu costs about 1000-1500 KSh. For trains, the SGR (Standard Gauge Railway) requires booking online at metickets.crbc.co.tz or via the official app. A second-class ticket from Nairobi to Mombasa is around 1000 KSh. Always book in advance during holidaysâChristmas and Easter fill up fast. When you arrive at the station, you'll need to show ID (passport for foreigners, national ID for locals). For matatus, you don't reserve; you just pay the conductor. But for long-distance buses, you can reserve a seat by phone. Say: 'Nataka kukata tikiti' (I want to buy a ticket). 'Nina nafasi?' (Do you have space?). 'Naweza kulipa kwa M-Pesa?' (Can I pay with M-Pesa?). M-Pesa is a mobile money serviceâwidely accepted. For flights, use apps like Skyscanner or local airlines like Precision Air, Jambojet, or RwandAir. A one-way flight from Dar es Salaam to Zanzibar can be as low as $50 if booked early. Keep your ticket safeâsome conductors check multiple times. If you need to change your ticket, ask: 'Naweza kubadilisha tikiti?' (Can I change my ticket?). Refunds are rare, so confirm dates. For reservations at hotels or safaris, use Booking.com or local tour operators. Always get a written confirmation via SMS or email. Tip: buy tickets from official counters to avoid scams.

lessons.title: At the Airport/Bus Station
lessons.body: Navigating an airport or bus station in East Africa requires patience and Swahili. At the airport, you'll first go to check-in. Show your passport and ticket. The agent will ask: 'Una mizigo mingapi?' (How many bags?). You'll place bags on the scale. Excess baggage costs extraâoften $10-20 per kilo. Then you go through security. They may ask you to remove shoes, belts, and laptops. After security, find your gate. Listen for announcements: 'Ndege ya kwenda Nairobi inaondoka sasa' (The plane to Nairobi is departing now). At bus stations, it's more chaotic. In Nairobi's Machakos or Mombasa's Mwembe Tayari, touts will shout destinations. Ignore them and go to the official ticket office. Ask: 'Basi la kwenda Arusha linaondoka saa ngapi?' (What time does the bus to Arusha leave?). Times are often in Swahili: saa moja (7 AM), saa mbili (8 AM), etc. Swahili time starts at 6 AM, so 7 AM is saa moja. For buses, you'll load your luggage in the hold. Keep your ticketâa conductor may check it. On board, you'll be given a seat number. If someone sits in your seat, say: 'Samahani, hii ni kiti changu' (Excuse me, this is my seat). At airports, after landing, you'll go through immigration. Have your visa or entry permit ready. Customs may ask: 'Una kitu cha kutangaza?' (Do you have anything to declare?). Then you collect your bags from the carousel. If your bag is lost, go to the airline desk and say: 'Mizigo yangu haipo' (My luggage is missing). Always keep your valuables with you. At bus stations, watch out for pickpockets. Use a money belt. If you need help, ask a uniformed official: 'Naweza kupata msaada?' (Can I get help?).

lessons.title: Asking for and Giving Directions
lessons.body: Getting lost in a Swahili-speaking area is easy, but asking for directions is straightforward. Start with a polite greeting: 'Samahani' (Excuse me). Then ask: 'Njia ya kwenda... iko wapi?' (Where is the way to...?). For example, 'Njia ya kwenda sokoni iko wapi?' (Where is the way to the market?). People will often reply with landmarks: 'Panda mlima' (Go up the hill), 'Shuka' (Go down), 'Kulia' (Turn right), 'Kushoto' (Turn left), 'Moja kwa moja' (Straight ahead). Distances are given in time: 'Dakika tano kwa miguu' (Five minutes on foot). If you need to confirm, repeat: 'Kulia? Kushoto?' (Right? Left?). In rural areas, directions might refer to trees, churches, or shops: 'Baada ya kanisa, pinduka kushoto' (After the church, turn left). If someone gives directions too fast, say: 'Tafadhali, polepole' (Please, slowly). To give directions, use the imperative: 'Nenda' (Go), 'Geuka' (Turn), 'Vuka barabara' (Cross the road). If you're giving directions to a taxi driver, say: 'Nipeleke kwenye...' (Take me to...). For example, 'Nipeleke kwenye hoteli ya Serena' (Take me to Serena Hotel). If you're on a boda boda, you might say: 'Pita hapa' (Pass here), 'Simama hapa' (Stop here). If you're lost, look for a petrol station or a shopâpeople there are used to giving directions. Avoid asking strangers at night. In cities, use Google Maps offlineâdownload the map before you go. But remember, many small streets aren't labeled. So combine tech with asking. Key phrases: 'Nimepotea' (I am lost), 'Niko wapi?' (Where am I?), 'Mbali?' (Is it far?). If someone says 'karibu' (welcome), they might be inviting you to their homeâpolitely decline if you're not comfortable. Always thank them: 'Asante sana' (Thank you very much).

lessons.title: Talking About Travel Plans
lessons.body: Talking about travel plans in Swahili helps you share your itinerary and make arrangements. Start with the future tense: 'Nitakwenda' (I will go), 'Tutasafiri' (We will travel). For example, 'Kesho nitakwenda Arusha' (Tomorrow I will go to Arusha). To ask about someone's plans: 'Utakwenda wapi?' (Where will you go?). 'Utabaki siku ngapi?' (How many days will you stay?). If you're planning a trip, you might say: 'Nataka kufanya safari' (I want to take a trip). 'Nina mpango wa kwenda Zanzibar' (I have a plan to go to Zanzibar). To discuss dates: 'Wiki ijayo' (Next week), 'Mwezi ujao' (Next month), 'Mwaka huu' (This year). For example, 'Nitakwenda Mombasa wiki ijayo' (I will go to Mombasa next week). If you're traveling with others: 'Tutasafiri pamoja' (We will travel together). To ask about cost: 'Safari itagharimu kiasi gani?' (How much will the trip cost?). To book: 'Nahitaji kukata tikiti' (I need to buy a ticket). If you're unsure: 'Labda nitakwenda' (Maybe I will go). To express a wish: 'Ningependa kwenda' (I would like to go). Use 'kwa' for transport: 'kwa basi' (by bus), 'kwa ndege' (by plane), 'kwa treni' (by train). For example, 'Nitakwenda kwa basi' (I will go by bus). To ask about duration: 'Safari itachukua muda gani?' (How long will the trip take?). Answers: 'Saa mbili' (Two hours), 'Siku moja' (One day). If you're inviting someone: 'Unataka kuja na mimi?' (Do you want to come with me?). To confirm: 'Tutaonana kesho' (We will see each other tomorrow). If plans change: 'Nimebadilisha mipango' (I have changed plans). Practice these phrases with a friend. Write your own travel plan in Swahili: 'Mwezi ujao, nitakwenda Nairobi kwa ndege. Nitakaa siku tatu. Nitakwenda kwenye makumbusho ya Nairobi.' This builds confidence. Remember, 'safari' means journey, so 'safari njema' means 'good journey'.

lessons.title: Cultural Tips: Travel Etiquette
lessons.body: Traveling in East Africa requires respecting local customs. Greetings are essential. Always greet before asking for anything. Say 'Jambo' or 'Habari' (Hello/How are you?). In Tanzania, 'Shikamoo' is for elders (they reply 'Marahaba'). In Kenya, 'Sasa' is casual. When you enter a shop or office, greet everyone. It's rude to jump straight to business. Dress modestly, especially in Muslim areas like Zanzibar or coastal towns. Women should cover shoulders and knees. Men should avoid shorts in rural areas. When eating, use your right hand. If offered food, accept a little even if you're not hungryâit's polite. In restaurants, tipping is not mandatory but appreciated (10% in tourist areas). For transport, if you're in a matatu and an elderly person boards, offer your seat. On buses, don't put your feet on the seat. When taking photos, ask first: 'Naweza kupiga picha?' (Can I take a photo?). Some people, especially in Maasai communities, may expect payment. Bargaining is normal in markets, but not in shops with fixed prices. Start at half the asking price and negotiate with a smile. Don't lose your temper. If invited to someone's home, bring a small gift like fruit or sugar. Remove your shoes before entering. When leaving, say 'Asante kwa mwaliko' (Thank you for the invitation). In business settings, handshakes are common. Use both hands or your right hand. Don't use your left hand to give or receive. Public displays of affection are frowned upon. Also, avoid pointing with your fingerâuse your whole hand. If you're in a village, ask permission before entering a homestead. Respect elders: stand when they enter, and listen more than you speak. Finally, learn a few words in local languages like Kikuyu, Luo, or Maasaiâit shows respect. 'Asante' works everywhere. If you make a mistake, apologize: 'Samahani, sikujua' (Sorry, I didn't know). People are forgiving if you try.

quiz.explanation: Matatu is a minibus taxi common in Kenya and Tanzania.
